notes.bp: A child learning to change articulation needs feedback that connects what they feel and see with how their speech sounds.
notes.wh: Articulation is hidden, children vary in development, and feedback must align audio, visual movement, and a usable teaching target without overwhelming the learner.
notes.naive: Show a waveform or give a generic pronunciation score and assume it identifies the movement to change.
notes.ap: Build a multimodal American English child-speech corpus specialized for articulatory feedback, with synchronized speech and articulatory information.
notes.mech: PERCEPT-US provides a multimodal child speech corpus designed for articulatory feedback.
notes.math: The corpus makes a hidden motor target observable: acoustic output can be related to articulator configuration and learner-facing feedback rather than treated as an isolated sound label.
notes.ww: The paper reports corpus resources and articulatory-feedback-oriented evaluation for American English child speech.
notes.limits: Speakers, ages, tasks, sensor alignment, labels, and corpus size limit generalization; a resource does not itself establish learning or clinical benefit.
notes.title: PERCEPT-US: A Multimodal American English Child Speech Corpus Specialized for Articulatory Feedback

notes.bp: Biometric anti-spoofing must reject attacks across modalities and conditions while staying light enough for real security systems.
notes.wh: Attack traces differ by sensor and generator, and a heavy multimodal model can be accurate but too slow or too specialized to deploy.
notes.naive: Train a modality-specific detector or use a large model and evaluate only on the attack types seen during training.
notes.ap: Combine lightweight modality-aware representations with generalized anti-spoofing features and test cross-condition biometric security.
notes.mech: LitMAS is a lightweight generalized multimodal anti-spoofing framework for biometric security.
notes.math: Security is a coverage problem: the model must learn signs of manipulation that survive changes in modality and attack source, while the resource budget constrains the detector itself.
notes.ww: The paper reports generalized multimodal anti-spoofing performance with a lightweight framework.
notes.limits: Biometric modalities, attacks, datasets, fusion, thresholds, and compute budget bound the result; benchmark generalization is not security certification.
notes.title: LitMAS: A Lightweight and Generalized Multi-Modal Anti-Spoofing Framework for Biometric Security

notes.bp: An ASR decoder must choose a likely word sequence efficiently, but beam search can miss a better path or spend too much computation on unhelpful alternatives.
notes.wh: Transducer scores are local while the best sequence is global; beam width, pruning, and length effects interact with streaming constraints.
notes.naive: Increase the beam indefinitely or use greedy decoding and assume the accuracy/latency tradeoff is universal.
notes.ap: Analyze and improve beam-search decoding for transducer ASR, testing how search choices affect accuracy and computation.
notes.mech: The paper pushes the limits of beam-search decoding for transducer-based ASR models.
notes.math: Decoding is an inference budget: the beam is a controlled approximation to sequence search, and improvements come from spending computation where competing hypotheses remain plausible.
notes.ww: The paper reports decoding accuracy and efficiency findings for transducer ASR across the tested search settings.
notes.limits: Model, language, beam policy, pruning, hardware, and streaming setup bound the result; a better beam does not remove acoustic or language-model errors.
notes.title: Pushing the Limits of Beam Search Decoding  for Transducer-based ASR models

notes.bp: A speech tokenizer should turn sound into compact units that preserve the information a downstream speech model actually needs.
notes.wh: Acoustic detail, phonetic identity, speaker identity, and temporal precision compete for a limited token budget; reconstruction quality alone may reward irrelevant detail.
notes.naive: Use waveform compression or text-like units and assume the best reconstruction tokenizer is the best speech representation.
notes.ap: Build a phonetic-acoustic tokenizer and evaluate whether its tokens capture both speech sound structure and useful phonetic distinctions.
notes.mech: PAST is a phonetic-acoustic speech tokenizer.
notes.math: Tokenization is a choice about what survives discretization: units should preserve acoustically grounded, phonetic information while discarding redundant waveform variation.
notes.ww: The paper reports tokenizer quality and downstream speech-representation results for the proposed phonetic-acoustic units.
notes.limits: Token rate, codebook, languages, speakers, reconstruction target, and downstream tasks bound the claim; discrete units are not automatically linguistically complete.
notes.title: PAST: Phonetic-Acoustic Speech Tokenizer

notes.bp: A dialogue-state tracker should use examples in context effectively, but its ability to learn from a few demonstrations may depend on how the dialogue and prompts are arranged.
notes.wh: State labels, turn order, domain vocabulary, and example selection can change what the model appears to infer from context.
notes.naive: Measure one prompt format and attribute the result to general in-context learning ability.
notes.ap: Systematically vary dialogue-state-tracking factors such as demonstrations, domain, and context to identify which conditions support or break in-context learning.
notes.mech: The paper studies factors affecting the in-context learning abilities of LLMs for dialogue state tracking.
notes.math: In-context learning is an interaction between model prior and task presentation: the examples are part of the effective program and must be analyzed as such.
notes.ww: The paper reports factor-level findings on in-context dialogue-state tracking.
notes.limits: Model family, prompt, domains, state schema, demonstration order, and context length bound the result; prompt sensitivity is not a stable conversational capability.
notes.title: Factors affecting the in-context learning abilities of LLMs for dialogue state tracking

notes.bp: Speech translation can use articulator movement as an intermediate signal, especially when the sound alone is ambiguous or the target language lacks data.
notes.wh: Articulator space is not directly observed in ordinary speech, and translation must preserve meaning while passing through a representation with its own measurement errors.
notes.naive: Translate acoustic features directly or force a text transcript and assume articulation adds nothing.
notes.ap: Build an end-to-end monolingual speech-translation system that represents speech in articulator space and tests whether the intermediate structure helps.
notes.mech: ArticulateX is an end-to-end monolingual speech translation system operating in articulator space.
notes.math: The proposed bridge changes the unit of translation: vocal-tract movement is treated as a structured intermediate constraint between sound and language.
notes.ww: The paper reports speech-translation results for the articulator-space system in its tested monolingual setting.
notes.limits: Language, corpus, articulatory estimation, model, references, and evaluation bound generalization; an intermediate representation is not proof of human-like translation.
notes.title: ArticulateX: End-to-End Monolingual Speech Translation in Articulator Space

notes.bp: An audio-visual system should identify the regions in a video associated with a sound, even for categories or scenes it did not see during training.
notes.wh: Audio and vision have different timing and semantics; zero-shot matching can confuse co-occurrence with the object that actually produced the sound.
notes.naive: Detect objects from vision alone or train a closed-set audiovisual segmenter and reject unseen categories.
notes.ap: Connect pretrained audio and vision models so shared representations can guide zero-shot audiovisual segmentation.
notes.mech: The paper studies zero-shot audiovisual segmentation by bridging pretrained audio and vision models.
notes.math: Segmentation is grounded association: the system must align a sound event with a spatial region using cross-modal evidence rather than merely classify the clip.
notes.ww: The paper reports zero-shot audiovisual segmentation results for the connected pretrained models.
notes.limits: Datasets, categories, synchronization, pretrained models, and segmentation labels bound the result; co-occurrence does not establish physical source identity.
notes.title: Bridging Audio and Vision: Zero-Shot Audiovisual Segmentation by Connecting Pretrained Models

notes.bp: A TTS system should make emphasis and emotion controllable together, because stressing a word changes how emotion is perceived and emotion changes which emphasis sounds natural.
notes.wh: Text, prosody, and affect are entangled; independent controls can conflict or produce an emphasized contour that does not fit the intended emotion.
notes.naive: Add an emotion label after synthesis or control pitch and energy independently with no relation to the emphasized word.
notes.ap: Model the link between emphasis and emotion explicitly so text position, prosody, and affect can be jointly controlled.
notes.mech: EME-TTS targets the emphasis-emotion link in speech synthesis.
notes.math: Expressive synthesis is a constrained coordination problem: emphasis is local and linguistic, emotion is broader and affective, and the system must make their interaction coherent.
notes.ww: The paper reports expressive TTS quality and controllability for emphasis and emotion in the tested evaluations.
notes.limits: Languages, speakers, labels, text prompts, control ranges, and subjective raters bound the claim; controllability does not guarantee natural or culturally appropriate expression.
notes.title: EME-TTS: Unlocking the Emphasis and Emotion Link in Speech Synthesis
